newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open higher, 2-yr note sale awaited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open higher, 2-yr note sale awaited.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries opened firmer on Tuesday, as the market used the lower prices after Monday's sell-off as an excuse to buy, traders said.
In early trading, the 30-year bond was at 99-7/32, up 8/32, with its yield at 6.69 percent.
"It is all Street driven," said a trader at a primary dealership of the bounce. "People are just covering shorts. There is no retail buying."
The market now sets its sights on this afternoon's auction, in which the Treasury will sell $15.5 billion of two-year notes.
The auction is expected to garner strong demand, in light of its small size. Until the results are released at 1345 EDT, players said Treasuries should stick to narrow ranges.
Some said dealers may try and cheapen up the issue to 6.05 percent, but that it is more likely the two-year would be sold at 6.02-6.03 percent.
Ahead of the auction, the when-issued two-year note was at 6.015 percent.
"It's really a non-event," said a trader. "It will come and go."

On Monday, traders talked of a likely concession, which occurred late in the day, after bearish remarks from Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto led to a sell-off. But the concession was erased early this morning, leading players to believe the market continues to benefit from excellent technicals.

Hashimoto spooked U.S. asset markets after he told a New York audience that Japan might be tempted to sell its U.S. Treasury securities if the dollar fell sharply. His remarks were seen as Japanese frustration over unstable dollar-yen exchange rates.
"(The comments) came at a quiet time; it was dead, and the market was looking for an excuse to get some action," said Joseph Liro, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp.
"It was late in the day so maybe it was an overreaction," added a trader. "It was a message to Clinton ... it leaves us with uncertainty."
Analysts said that Japan has no choice but to continue to buy U.S. Treasuries as they recycle dollars they receive due to their huge trade surplus with the U.S.

Meanwhile, Tuesday's economic data are not expected to move the market much. At 1000 EDT, the Conference Board is slated to release its consumer confidence figures for June. Economists expect the index to remain close to its high of 127 seen in May.

Liro said the consumer is in good shape, helped by strong job and income growth. "After a second quarter pause I expect consumers to reassert themselves in the third quarter," he said, adding that the spending would likely be in non-durable goods.
In early trading, the three-month bill rate was down six basis points at 4.98 percent. Six-month bills were down two basis points at 5.07 percent and year-bills were unchanged at 5.34 percent.

Two-year notes were at 100-13/32, up 1/32, to yield 6.02 percent. Five-year notes were up 3/32 at 100-28/32, yielding 6.29 percent, and 10-year notes were at 101-20/32, up 5/32, yielding 6.40 percent.
